blurb: Cuba's national dog, a silky-coated bichon with a springy, lively gait
description: The Havanese is a small bichon-type toy dog from Cuba with a long, soft, silky coat, a springy gait and a friendly, easily trained nature.
answer: The Havanese is a bichon-type toy dog and the national dog of Cuba, developed from the extinct Blanquito de la Habana. It stands about 22–29 cm, has a long, silky coat, and is known for its friendly, readily trained nature.

body: The breed belongs to the bichon family. Its ancestors probably came to Cuba from Tenerife aboard Spanish ships, and the Blanquito de la Habana that developed there is thought to have been crossed with other bichon types, including the poodle. These dogs became companions to Spanish colonists and Cuban nobility.

After the Cuban Revolution few emigrants could bring their dogs, and when American breeders took an interest in the 1970s the US gene pool was only 11 dogs. The AKC recognised the breed in 1996, and it has since become one of the faster-growing breeds in registrations.

The Havanese stands 22–29 cm, ideally 23–27 cm, and is slightly longer than tall, with a topline that rises slightly toward the croup and a springy gait. The tail arches over the back and the eyes are dark and almond-shaped. The long double coat is soft, light, silky and slightly wavy; the undercoat may be absent. All colors are accepted, and the coat may be brushed out or corded.

The breed is described as friendly and readily trained, which has made it popular for work with the public as therapy dogs, hearing-signal dogs and performers, and in mold and termite detection and tracking.

Havanese take part in agility, flyball, canine freestyle and obedience. For the show ring they are kept untrimmed apart from tidying the feet, so the long coat generally needs regular brushing or cord maintenance.

A 2024 UK study of 56 dogs found a life expectancy of 14.5 years. Conditions reported in the breed include luxating patella, liver disease, heart disease, cataracts, retinal dysplasia, sebaceous adenitis and portosystemic shunt.
